title: Read an offer before you answer
header_line: My analysis of one book on negotiation. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Why is someone offering you business out of the blue?

A student described an unexpected offer of work from a contact, introduced three ways. I said that the offer arrived suddenly from a party who had never done it before, and asked the group to think about what the offer might be doing.
I said that a surprise like that can be a distraction, a way to see whether you are greedy enough to take business that competes with a partner of yours.
I said: I told him, I have never really heard anything about you, tell me a little about yourself. You have to be careful not to question too much.
I said it takes practice: at the beginning it sounds cagey and rehearsed, but you have to feel the moment on the call or in person, and say: I would love to learn about your story.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write an unexpected offer you received.
Write what the offer might be for.
Write three questions to learn about the sender.
Write what you will not decide on the first call.
Write who you would ask for a second view.

check.q: What did I say a surprise offer could be?
choices: A way to test whether you will take competing business

check.q: What did I say to ask?
choices: Tell me a little about yourself

check.q: What did I say about practice?
choices: It sounds cagey at first and improves

recap: Read a surprise offer. Ask before you answer.
